```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(BonusLab)
library(caret)
library(mlbench)
```

This vignette shows how to do a simple prediction problem using the
`ridgereg()` function together with the `caret` package. We model the median
house value (`medv`) in the `BostonHousing` data from the `mlbench` package.

## 1. Divide the data into a training and a test set

```{r data}
data("BostonHousing")
str(BostonHousing)
```

We use `caret::createDataPartition()` to put 80% of the observations in the
training set and the remaining 20% in the test set. The split is stratified on
the response-variable `medv`, so both sets get a similar distribution of house values.

```{r split}
set.seed(12345)
train_index <- createDataPartition(BostonHousing$medv, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)

train_data <- BostonHousing[train_index, ]
test_data <- BostonHousing[-train_index, ]

dim(train_data)
dim(test_data)
```

## 2. Fit a linear regression model and a model with forward selection

All models in this vignette are tuned and compared with 10-fold
cross-validation. We create the folds once and reuse them for every model, so
all models are evaluated on exactly the same splits of the training data.

```{r folds}
set.seed(12345)
# create folds-indexes, strata medv
folds <- createFolds(train_data$medv, k = 10, returnTrain = TRUE)
 # Put them into list object meant for caret::train
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, index = folds)
```

### Linear regression

The first model is an ordinary linear regression with all 13 covariates.

```{r lm}
lm_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train_data, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
lm_fit
```

### Linear regression with forward selection

For forward selection we use `method = "leapForward"` (from the `leaps`
package). Its tuning parameter `nvmax` is the number of covariates in the
model. By default `caret` only tries a few values of `nvmax`, so we give it
the full grid `1:13` to make sure every model size can be selected.

```{r forward}
forward_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train_data, method = "leapForward",
                     trControl = ctrl, tuneGrid = data.frame(nvmax = 1:13))
forward_fit 
```

`leapForward` always includes at least one covariate, so the intercept-only
model (0 covariates) is not part of the grid. We compute its cross-validated
RMSE by hand on the same folds. The intercept-only model predicts the mean of
the training fold for every observation in the held-out fold.

```{r intercept-only}
# Intercept only "model"
rmse_intercept_only <- sapply(folds, function(idx) {
  held_out <- train_data[-idx, ]
  # RMSE = sqrt(mean((y_true - y_pred)^2)), 10-fold CV
  sqrt(mean((held_out$medv - mean(train_data$medv[idx]))^2))
})

forward_rmse <- data.frame(
  covariates = 0:13,
  RMSE = c(mean(rmse_intercept_only), forward_fit$results$RMSE)
)
forward_rmse |> round(3)
```

The model with the lowest cross-validated RMSE among all sizes 0 to 13 is:

```{r forward-best}
forward_rmse[which.min(forward_rmse$RMSE), ] |> round(3)
```

which is the same coefficients that `caret` chose. The intercept-only model is
far worse than all the others. The selected covariates and their coefficients
are

```{r forward-coef}
coef(forward_fit$finalModel, forward_fit$bestTune$nvmax) |> round(3)
```

## 3. Evaluate the performance on the training set

`train()` refits the selected model on the whole training.
So we use `predict()`  to give us the fitted values on training data.
`caret::postResample()` computes RMSE, $R^2$ and MAE from the predicted
and observed values.

```{r train-performance}
train_performance <- rbind(
  lm = postResample(predict(lm_fit, train_data), train_data$medv),
  forward = postResample(predict(forward_fit, train_data), train_data$medv)
)
train_performance |> round(3)
```

Both models explain about 71% of the variance in `medv` on the training data.
The full model has a slightly lower training RMSE. Which makes sense, as
adding covariates to a linear regression can never increase the training error.
If we look at the cross-validated RMSE from step 2, it is an
estimate of the error on "new data", and it is higher for both models.

```{r train-vs-cv}
data.frame(
  train_RMSE = train_performance[, "RMSE"],
  cv_RMSE = c(lm_fit$results$RMSE, min(forward_fit$results$RMSE)),
  row.names = c("lm", "forward")
) |> round(3)
```

The ranking then flips. The full model is best on the training data, but the
forward selection model is best in cross-validation.

## 4. Fit ridge regression models with `ridgereg()` for different values of lambda

### A custom `caret` model for `ridgereg()`

`ridgereg()` is not one of the built-in models in `caret`, but `train()` also
accepts a list that describes a custom model. The list tells `caret` what the
tuning parameter is, how to create a default grid of values, how to fit the
model and how to predict with it.

```{r ridgereg-caret}
ridgereg_caret <- list(
  label = "Ridge regression with ridgereg()",
  library = "BonusLab",
  type = "Regression",
  # lambda is the only tuning parameter
  parameters = data.frame(parameter = "lambda", class = "numeric",
                          label = "lambda"),
  # default grid, lambda on a log scale between 0.01 and 1000
  grid = function(x, y, len = NULL, search = "grid") {
    if (search == "grid") {
      data.frame(lambda = 10^seq(-2, 3, length.out = len))
    } else {
      data.frame(lambda = 10^stats::runif(len, min = -2, max = 3))
    }
  },
  # caret gives the covariates as a matrix x and the response as a vector y
  fit = function(x, y, wts, param, lev, last, classProbs, ...) {
    dat <- as.data.frame(x)
    dat$.outcome <- y
    ridgereg(.outcome ~ ., data = dat, lambda = param$lambda)
  },
  predict = function(modelFit, newdata, preProc = NULL, submodels = NULL) {
    predict(modelFit, newdata = as.data.frame(newdata))
  },
  prob = NULL,
  # from the simplest model (largest lambda) to the most complex
  sort = function(x) x[order(-x$lambda), , drop = FALSE]
)
```

`ridgereg()` normalizes the covariates itself, so no pre-processing is needed
in `caret`.

### Fitting for different values of lambda

To see what lambda does, we fit the model on the whole training set for different
values of lambda.

```{r ridgereg-lambdas}
lambdas <- c(0, 1, 10, 100, 1000)

ridge_fits <- lapply(lambdas, function(l) {
  train(medv ~ ., data = train_data, method = ridgereg_caret,
        # trainControl(method = "none") to fit on traindata, no cv
        trControl = trainControl(method = "none"),
        tuneGrid = data.frame(lambda = l))
})
```

As lambda grows, the coefficients are shrunk towards zero.

```{r ridgereg-coef}
ridge_coef <- sapply(ridge_fits, function(fit) coef(fit$finalModel))
dimnames(ridge_coef) <- list(colnames(coef(ridge_fits[[1]]$finalModel)),
                             paste0("lambda=", lambdas))
round(ridge_coef, 3)
```

With `lambda = 0` the model is an ordinary linear regression, so it has the
same training performance as `lm_fit`. A larger lambda gives a simpler model
with a higher training error. Whether that simpler model is better on new data
is decided with cross-validation.

```{r ridgereg-train-performance}
sapply(ridge_fits, function(fit) {
  postResample(predict(fit, train_data), train_data$medv)
}) |>
  t() |>
  round(3) |>
  `rownames<-`(paste0("lambda=", lambdas))
```

## 5. Find the best lambda with 10-fold cross-validation

We now let `train()` choose lambda. It uses the same 10 folds as the models in
step 2 (through `ctrl`), so the cross-validated errors of all three models are
directly comparable. Then we add a tune-grid that contains `lambda = 0` (ordinary linear
regression) and 25 values on a log scale between 0.1 and 1000.

```{r ridgereg-cv}
lambda_grid <- data.frame(lambda = c(0, 10^seq(-1, 3, length.out = 25)))

# fit model, with cv 10-fold as defined in ctrl, and tuneGrid for lambda
ridge_fit <- train(medv ~ ., data = train_data, method = ridgereg_caret,
                   trControl = ctrl, tuneGrid = lambda_grid)
# best lambda in grid (lowest RMSE in cross-validation)
ridge_fit$bestTune
```

The cross-validated RMSE as a function of lambda (best lambda indicated with red line):

```{r ridgereg-cv-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
cv_results <- ridge_fit$results[ridge_fit$results$lambda > 0, ]

ggplot2::ggplot(cv_results, ggplot2::aes(x = lambda, y = RMSE)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = ridge_fit$bestTune$lambda,
                      linetype = "dashed", color = "red") + # at 15 ish
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "lambda (log scale)", y = "Cross-validated RMSE") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()
```

For small values of lambda the model is almost the same as the ordinary
linear regression, and the curve is flat. The RMSE has a shallow minimum
around the selected lambda, and for large values of lambda the coefficients
are shrunk too much and the error increases quickly.

`train()` has refitted the model with the best lambda on the whole training
set. Comparing the cross-validated RMSE of the three models:

```{r cv-comparison}
data.frame(
  model = c("lm", "forward", "ridgereg"),
  cv_RMSE = c(min(lm_fit$results$RMSE),
              min(forward_fit$results$RMSE),
              min(ridge_fit$results$RMSE))
)
```

The differences are small. Ridge regression is slightly better than the
ordinary linear regression, but the forward selection model has the lowest
cross-validated RMSE.

## 6. Evaluate all three models on the test set

For each model we use the final model that `train()` refitted on the whole
training set, predict `medv` for the `r nrow(test_data)` observations in the
test set and compute the RMSE with `caret::RMSE()`.

```{r test-comparison}
test_rmse <- data.frame(
  model = c("lm", "forward", "ridgereg"),
  test_RMSE = c(
    RMSE(predict(lm_fit, newdata = test_data), test_data$medv),
    RMSE(predict(forward_fit, newdata = test_data), test_data$medv),
    RMSE(predict(ridge_fit, newdata = test_data), test_data$medv)
  )
)
knitr::kable(test_rmse, digits = 3)
```

The forward selection model has the lowest test RMSE, followed closely by the
ordinary linear regression, while the ridge regression model is slightly
worse. This is the same winner as in the cross-validation, but ridge
regression and the linear regression have switched places.
